screens.title: Amazon EFS and FSx: Shared File Systems
screens.narratorSegment: Shared file systems let many compute resources access the same files at the same time using standard file protocols. In AWS, Amazon EFS and the FSx family provide managed shared file storage for Linux and Windows workloads, and for high-performance parallel workloads. In this lesson you will learn why shared file systems exist, when to pick EFS versus FSx variants, and how performance and throughput settings change behavior. We will also walk through securing EFS mounts and a practical terminal demo for mounting a file system to an EC2 instance. As you study, watch for common architecture mistakes: using object storage where POSIX semantics are required, or using single-instance block storage when multiple servers need concurrent access. By the end of this chapter you will be able to select the right AWS storage service for typical enterprise and HPC scenarios, and perform the basic steps to create and mount an EFS file system. Think about an application you manage: does it need POSIX semantics, Windows-native features, or extreme parallel throughput? That question will guide your choice.

Amazon EFS and FSx: Shared File Systems

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus your practice. First, you will explain Amazon EFS use cases and architectural benefits, which means you can identify when shared POSIX semantics are required and why multi-AZ durability matters. Second, you will differentiate EFS performance and throughput modes so you can match mode choices to workload patterns and avoid surprises under load. Third, you will understand EFS security and access control mechanisms including mount targets, security groups, IAM, access points, and encryption options, so you can implement least-privilege access for applications. Fourth, you will describe FSx options — Windows File Server and Lustre — and when to choose each based on protocol and performance needs. Each objective links practical steps with architecture rationale. For example, knowing when to use provisioned throughput avoids underperforming file systems for steady high-throughput workloads. A quick misconception to avoid: shared file systems are not a one-size-fits-all replacement for object or block storage. Keep the workload access pattern and OS protocol needs front and center as you progress.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Objective Checklist
01 — EFS use case test
Can your app use NFS, and does it require POSIX semantics? If yes, EFS is a candidate. If you need HTTP access or objects at scale, S3 is better.
02 — Performance match
If your workload is latency-sensitive per-file, choose General Purpose. If aggregate throughput for parallel jobs matters, consider Max I/O or FSx for Lustre.
03 — Security checklist
Ensure mount targets in required AZs, lock NFS port 2049 to EC2 security groups, enable access points for app-level control, and enable encryption as needed.
04 — FSx selection guide
If Windows features like NTFS and AD are needed, choose FSx for Windows. For HPC throughput and S3 integration, choose FSx for Lustre.

screens.title: What is a shared file system?
screens.narratorSegment: A shared file system is a storage system that multiple compute instances can mount and access at the same time using a standard file protocol. That means processes on different servers can open, read, write, and lock the same files with familiar POSIX or native file semantics. Think of it like a shared office filing cabinet: multiple coworkers can open the same drawer and work on documents, provided they coordinate access. In AWS, shared file systems give you that capability without managing the underlying servers. A concrete example is a web cluster where multiple Linux EC2 instances serve and modify uploaded content in a common directory. If you used EBS block storage for each instance, that content would be isolated on a single instance and not shareable. A common misconception is to confuse shared file systems with object storage. Object stores like S3 do not preserve POSIX semantics like file locking or atomic renames; they are accessed via HTTP APIs and are suited for different patterns. Key takeaway: choose a shared file system when your application requires multiple servers to operate on the same file tree with standard file semantics. How would your application behave if two servers concurrently renamed or truncated the same file? That test reveals whether you need a shared file system.

keyIdea.text: Shared file systems let many servers use the same file namespace with standard file semantics; choose them when concurrent file operations are required.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is a shared file system?
Shared file system explained
A multi-client filesystem providing concurrent access with standard file semantics like read, write, and locks.
Analogy: a shared office filing cabinet that many coworkers can use while coordinating access.
Concrete example: multiple web servers mounting a common directory for user-uploaded content and sessions.
Misconception: object storage is not a drop-in replacement when POSIX semantics are required.
Visual checklist
  • Multiple clients mount the same namespace concurrently.
  • Applications rely on file semantics for coordination.
  • Low-latency metadata operations may be important.
Key Takeaway

Use shared file systems when concurrent file access and POSIX semantics are required across servers.

screens.title: Amazon EFS — managed elastic NFS
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system designed for scalable, concurrent access by thousands of EC2 instances. Its elasticity means the system grows and shrinks as files are added and removed, so you don't provision capacity up front. Architecturally, EFS stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones in a region to provide high availability and durability. Mount targets are network interfaces within each AZ where EC2 instances connect over NFS. EFS is ideal for lift-and-shift of Linux-based applications that relied on an on-premises NFS server, for container workloads needing shared persistent storage, and for content management systems that require concurrent access. A concrete example: a containerized CMS where each task pod mounts the same EFS share for uploaded assets; the share scales without manual resizing. A common misconception is to expect EFS to perform like local disk in every scenario; EFS is networked storage and latency-sensitive operations should be evaluated. Key takeaway: EFS removes capacity management and adds multi-AZ durability, but you must design for network latency and mount target placement in AZs where your compute runs. Amazon EFS — managed elastic NFS means efs offers elastic, multi-az nfs storage for concurrent linux workloads; plan mount targets and evaluate latency expectations.. In practical terms, how efs provides elastic capacity, multi-az durability, and concurrent mounts.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: EFS offers elastic, multi-AZ NFS storage for concurrent Linux workloads; plan mount targets and evaluate latency expectations.

content.html:
Definition › Amazon EFS
EFS architecture at a glance
Managed NFS, automatic capacity scaling, and multi-AZ redundancy for durability and availability.
Mount targets: network interfaces in each Availability Zone to which EC2 instances connect.
Elastic capacity: storage grows and shrinks with your data, avoiding manual provisioning.
Use cases: shared home directories, web servers, container persistent storage.
Example scenario
A fleet of Linux EC2 instances runs a CMS and mounts an EFS file system for user uploads. As traffic grows, storage grows automatically and remains available across AZ failures.
Key Takeaway

EFS simplifies shared storage for Linux workloads but requires network-aware architecture and mount target placement.

screens.title: EFS Performance Modes
screens.narratorSegment: EFS provides two performance modes that change how the file system optimizes latency and aggregate IOPS. General Purpose is the default and is tuned for low latency on individual file operations; it suits web servers, home directories, and most general workloads. Max input and output is designed for extreme parallelism and very high aggregate throughput and IOPS; it scales better for workloads like big data analytics, media processing, or genomics that run thousands of clients in parallel. An important practical example: a multi-node analytics job that opens many files concurrently may see better total throughput in Max input and output, but each single file operation might incur slightly higher latency. A common misconception is that Max input and output always performs better; it trades per-operation latency for aggregate scalability. When choosing, evaluate whether your application needs fast single-file responses or massive parallel throughput. To decide, profile typical file operation latency and measure aggregate input and output under realistic concurrency. Key takeaway: pick General Purpose for latency-sensitive tasks and Max input and output when parallel throughput dominates your workload. EFS Performance Modes means general purpose favors low latency; max i/o favors aggregate throughput for highly parallel workloads.. In practical terms, general purpose versus max i/o — balance latency and aggregate throughput.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: General Purpose favors low latency; Max I/O favors aggregate throughput for highly parallel workloads.

content.html:
Comparison › EFS Performance Modes
General Purpose
Balanced performance with lower per-operation latency. Ideal for web serving and interactive workloads.
Use case: user-facing CMS where single-file reads must be quick.
Behavior: lower latency, suitable for typical file-system semantics.
Max I/O
Optimized for very high aggregate IOPS and throughput when many clients operate in parallel.
Use case: large-scale analytics or media transcoding across hundreds of nodes.
Misconception: not always lower latency; single-operation latency can be slightly higher.
Decision check
If single-request latency matters, choose General Purpose.
Decision check
If aggregate throughput at high concurrency matters, choose Max I/O.
Key Takeaway
Match mode to whether latency or aggregate throughput is the dominant requirement.

screens.title: EFS Throughput Modes
screens.narratorSegment: EFS offers two throughput modes that determine how read and write throughput scales. Bursting Throughput is the default. Throughput scales with the amount of data stored: larger file systems get a higher baseline and can burst above that baseline for short periods. This makes bursting the most cost-effective option for workloads with intermittent peaks, such as dev/test environments or sites with variable traffic. Provisioned Throughput lets you set a fixed throughput independent of the stored data size. Use this when your workload needs consistent high throughput but does not store large amounts of data — for example, a steady high-traffic media processing pipeline. A common mistake is assuming bursting handles sustained high throughput; if your workload constantly needs high bandwidth while storing little data, bursting may throttle you. Example: if an application stores only 10 gigabytes but processes hundreds of megabytes per second continuously, use provisioned throughput to avoid degraded performance. Key takeaway: choose bursting for typical, size-scaled throughput; choose provisioned when steady, predictable throughput is required regardless of stored data size. EFS Throughput Modes means bursting scales with stored data and works for variable workloads; provisioned gives predictable throughput independent of size.. In practical terms, bursting versus provisioned throughput and when to use each.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Bursting scales with stored data and works for variable workloads; provisioned gives predictable throughput independent of size.

content.html:
Process Flow › EFS Throughput Modes
Bursting Throughput
Throughput tied to size of file system; cost-effective for workloads with bursts.
• Baseline scales with stored data size.
• Good for intermittent heavy I/O followed by idle periods.
• Misconception: not ideal for sustained high throughput with small storage.
Provisioned Throughput
Set a fixed throughput level independent of storage size for predictable performance.
• Use when you need consistent high throughput but don't store much data.
• Ensures predictable performance for streaming or pipeline workloads.
• Misconception: costs are higher; use only when necessary.
Decision example
10 GB stored with constant 200 MB/s processing → Provisioned throughput recommended.
Key Takeaway
Match throughput mode to whether bandwidth needs scale with stored data or are steady and independent.

screens.title: EFS Security and Access Control
screens.narratorSegment: Securing an EFS file system requires layered controls. Network access first: EFS uses mount targets—elastic network interfaces in each Availability Zone—that clients connect to over NFS port 2049. Use security groups to restrict which EC2 instances or on-premises addresses can reach the mount target. IAM controls and EFS Access Points provide application-level controls; access points let you enforce a POSIX identity and path into the file system so different applications have isolated views and permissions. Encryption protects data at rest and in transit: at-rest encryption uses KMS-managed keys, while encryption in transit uses TLS between client and mount helper. A practical example: create mount targets in the AZs where your compute runs, open security group 2049 only to the EC2 group, and create access points for each application so file ownership and root directories are consistent. A common mistake is to expose NFS widely by opening 2049 to large CIDR ranges; that undermines purpose of access controls. Key takeaway: combine network-level controls, access points, IAM, and encryption rather than relying on a single mechanism. EFS Security and Access Control means use mount targets and security groups for network control, access points and iam for application-level access, and encryption for data protection.. In practical terms, mount targets, security groups, iam, access points, and encryption combine to secure efs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security layers
keyIdea.text: Use mount targets and security groups for network control, access points and IAM for application-level access, and encryption for data protection.

content.html:
Core Concept › EFS Security
Network controls
Mount targets provide AZ-local endpoints; secure NFS port 2049 with security groups and restrict access to known compute resources.
• Create mount targets in each AZ used by compute.
• Authorize only EC2 security groups that need access.
Application controls
Access Points let you define a POSIX identity and a restricted path per application to simplify permissions.
• Use access points for per-application isolation.
• Use IAM to control who can create or change file systems and access points.
Encryption at rest
Use KMS-managed keys to protect stored data.
Encryption in transit
Use TLS when mounting with the EFS mount helper to encrypt NFS traffic.
Key Takeaway
Apply layered controls: network, access points, IAM, and encryption together for robust protection.

screens.title: Creating an EFS File System (Console & CLI)
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an EFS file system involves selecting availability, performance, throughput, and security settings. In the console, you choose Regional availability, pick the VPC where your EC2 instances run, and typically keep General Purpose performance and Bursting throughput for general workloads. Enable encryption at rest if required. Configure mount targets by ensuring the file system creates them in the AZs where your EC2 instances run and attach security groups that allow NFS traffic only from authorized instances. For repeatable workflows, the CLI supports a simplified creation command that sets performance and throughput modes; additional steps create mount targets and authorize security group ingress. A practical CLI example in many labs is: aws efs create-file-system --performance-mode generalPurpose --throughput-mode bursting --encrypted. After creation, create mount targets for each AZ and adjust security groups. A common mistake is forgetting mount targets in the AZ of the EC2 instance, which makes the file system unreachable from that instance. Key takeaway: create the file system, set modes, and ensure mount targets and security group rules align with your compute placement. In practical terms, essential configuration steps and a simplified cli example.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Create EFS File System
Essential steps
  1. Choose Regional availability and select your VPC.
  2. Select Performance Mode (General Purpose or Max I/O).
  3. Select Throughput Mode (Bursting or Provisioned).
  4. Enable encryption at rest if required and create mount targets in AZs.

screens.title: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

screens.title: Amazon FSx for Lustre

screens.title: Choosing between S3, EBS, EFS, and FSx
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right storage service depends on protocol requirements, access patterns, and operating system needs. Amazon S3 is object storage accessed via HTTP and is ideal for unstructured content, backups, and data lakes where POSIX semantics are not required. Amazon EBS is block storage attached to a single EC2 instance, offering low-latency block device semantics for operating systems and databases. Amazon EFS is a shared NFS file system for Linux workloads needing concurrent POSIX file access and multi-AZ durability. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB and Windows-native features, while FSx for Lustre serves parallel, high-throughput compute clusters. A concrete decision example: a relational database needs EBS for single-instance block access; a web cluster serving uploaded images that require POSIX semantics uses EFS; a Windows file share with AD-integrated permissions uses FSx for Windows; an HPC job processing petabytes in parallel with S3-backed datasets uses FSx for Lustre. A common mistake is picking S3 because of cost without recognizing that the application expects POSIX behavior like atomic renames. Key takeaway: match protocol and semantics first, then performance profile, and finally cost and management trade-offs.

fullNarratorScript:
Shared file systems let many compute resources access the same files at the same time using standard file protocols. In AWS, Amazon EFS and the FSx family provide managed shared file storage for Linux and Windows workloads, and for high-performance parallel workloads. In this lesson you will learn why shared file systems exist, when to pick EFS versus FSx variants, and how performance and throughput settings change behavior. We will also walk through securing EFS mounts and a practical terminal demo for mounting a file system to an EC2 instance. As you study, watch for common architecture mistakes: using object storage where POSIX semantics are required, or using single-instance block storage when multiple servers need concurrent access. By the end of this chapter you will be able to select the right AWS storage service for typical enterprise and HPC scenarios, and perform the basic steps to create and mount an EFS file system. Think about an application you manage: does it need POSIX semantics, Windows-native features, or extreme parallel throughput? That question will guide your choice.

These learning objectives focus your practice. First, you will explain Amazon EFS use cases and architectural benefits, which means you can identify when shared POSIX semantics are required and why multi-AZ durability matters. Second, you will differentiate EFS performance and throughput modes so you can match mode choices to workload patterns and avoid surprises under load. Third, you will understand EFS security and access control mechanisms including mount targets, security groups, IAM, access points, and encryption options, so you can implement least-privilege access for applications. Fourth, you will describe FSx options — Windows File Server and Lustre — and when to choose each based on protocol and performance needs. Each objective links practical steps with architecture rationale. For example, knowing when to use provisioned throughput avoids underperforming file systems for steady high-throughput workloads. A quick misconception to avoid: shared file systems are not a one-size-fits-all replacement for object or block storage. Keep the workload access pattern and OS protocol needs front and center as you progress.

This screen expands the objectives into practical checks and why each matters. When you explain EFS use cases, you should be able to pick EFS instead of S3 or EBS for POSIX-dependent web apps. For performance modes, you should identify workloads where aggregate throughput matters more than single-operation latency. For security, you must be able to design mount targets in the right Availability Zones and open NFS port access only to authorized EC2 security groups. For FSx, practice mapping Windows application requirements to FSx for Windows File Server and mapping HPC or machine learning batch jobs to FSx for Lustre. A helpful misconception to avoid is assuming encryption at rest is a substitute for network controls; both are needed together. These practical outcomes turn a theoretical objective into something you can test in a lab or architecture review. Use these milestone checks as a short rubric for your own practice and to evaluate whether a chosen storage solution truly matches an application’s needs.

A shared file system is a storage system that multiple compute instances can mount and access at the same time using a standard file protocol. That means processes on different servers can open, read, write, and lock the same files with familiar POSIX or native file semantics. Think of it like a shared office filing cabinet: multiple coworkers can open the same drawer and work on documents, provided they coordinate access. In AWS, shared file systems give you that capability without managing the underlying servers. A concrete example is a web cluster where multiple Linux EC2 instances serve and modify uploaded content in a common directory. If you used EBS block storage for each instance, that content would be isolated on a single instance and not shareable. A common misconception is to confuse shared file systems with object storage. Object stores like S3 do not preserve POSIX semantics like file locking or atomic renames; they are accessed via HTTP APIs and are suited for different patterns. Key takeaway: choose a shared file system when your application requires multiple servers to operate on the same file tree with standard file semantics. How would your application behave if two servers concurrently renamed or truncated the same file? That test reveals whether you need a shared file system.

Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system designed for scalable, concurrent access by thousands of EC2 instances. Its elasticity means the system grows and shrinks as files are added and removed, so you don't provision capacity up front. Architecturally, EFS stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones in a region to provide high availability and durability. Mount targets are network interfaces within each AZ where EC2 instances connect over NFS. EFS is ideal for lift-and-shift of Linux-based applications that relied on an on-premises NFS server, for container workloads needing shared persistent storage, and for content management systems that require concurrent access. A concrete example: a containerized CMS where each task pod mounts the same EFS share for uploaded assets; the share scales without manual resizing. A common misconception is to expect EFS to perform like local disk in every scenario; EFS is networked storage and latency-sensitive operations should be evaluated. Key takeaway: EFS removes capacity management and adds multi-AZ durability, but you must design for network latency and mount target placement in AZs where your compute runs. Amazon EFS — managed elastic NFS means efs offers elastic, multi-az nfs storage for concurrent linux workloads; plan mount targets and evaluate latency expectations.. In practical terms, how efs provides elastic capacity, multi-az durability, and concurrent mounts.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EFS provides two performance modes that change how the file system optimizes latency and aggregate IOPS. General Purpose is the default and is tuned for low latency on individual file operations; it suits web servers, home directories, and most general workloads. Max input and output is designed for extreme parallelism and very high aggregate throughput and IOPS; it scales better for workloads like big data analytics, media processing, or genomics that run thousands of clients in parallel. An important practical example: a multi-node analytics job that opens many files concurrently may see better total throughput in Max input and output, but each single file operation might incur slightly higher latency. A common misconception is that Max input and output always performs better; it trades per-operation latency for aggregate scalability. When choosing, evaluate whether your application needs fast single-file responses or massive parallel throughput. To decide, profile typical file operation latency and measure aggregate input and output under realistic concurrency. Key takeaway: pick General Purpose for latency-sensitive tasks and Max input and output when parallel throughput dominates your workload. EFS Performance Modes means general purpose favors low latency; max i/o favors aggregate throughput for highly parallel workloads.. In practical terms, general purpose versus max i/o — balance latency and aggregate throughput.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EFS offers two throughput modes that determine how read and write throughput scales. Bursting Throughput is the default. Throughput scales with the amount of data stored: larger file systems get a higher baseline and can burst above that baseline for short periods. This makes bursting the most cost-effective option for workloads with intermittent peaks, such as dev/test environments or sites with variable traffic. Provisioned Throughput lets you set a fixed throughput independent of the stored data size. Use this when your workload needs consistent high throughput but does not store large amounts of data — for example, a steady high-traffic media processing pipeline. A common mistake is assuming bursting handles sustained high throughput; if your workload constantly needs high bandwidth while storing little data, bursting may throttle you. Example: if an application stores only 10 gigabytes but processes hundreds of megabytes per second continuously, use provisioned throughput to avoid degraded performance. Key takeaway: choose bursting for typical, size-scaled throughput; choose provisioned when steady, predictable throughput is required regardless of stored data size. EFS Throughput Modes means bursting scales with stored data and works for variable workloads; provisioned gives predictable throughput independent of size.. In practical terms, bursting versus provisioned throughput and when to use each.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Securing an EFS file system requires layered controls. Network access first: EFS uses mount targets—elastic network interfaces in each Availability Zone—that clients connect to over NFS port 2049. Use security groups to restrict which EC2 instances or on-premises addresses can reach the mount target. IAM controls and EFS Access Points provide application-level controls; access points let you enforce a POSIX identity and path into the file system so different applications have isolated views and permissions. Encryption protects data at rest and in transit: at-rest encryption uses KMS-managed keys, while encryption in transit uses TLS between client and mount helper. A practical example: create mount targets in the AZs where your compute runs, open security group 2049 only to the EC2 group, and create access points for each application so file ownership and root directories are consistent. A common mistake is to expose NFS widely by opening 2049 to large CIDR ranges; that undermines purpose of access controls. Key takeaway: combine network-level controls, access points, IAM, and encryption rather than relying on a single mechanism. EFS Security and Access Control means use mount targets and security groups for network control, access points and iam for application-level access, and encryption for data protection.. In practical terms, mount targets, security groups, iam, access points, and encryption combine to secure efs.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating an EFS file system involves selecting availability, performance, throughput, and security settings. In the console, you choose Regional availability, pick the VPC where your EC2 instances run, and typically keep General Purpose performance and Bursting throughput for general workloads. Enable encryption at rest if required. Configure mount targets by ensuring the file system creates them in the AZs where your EC2 instances run and attach security groups that allow NFS traffic only from authorized instances. For repeatable workflows, the CLI supports a simplified creation command that sets performance and throughput modes; additional steps create mount targets and authorize security group ingress. A practical CLI example in many labs is: aws efs create-file-system --performance-mode generalPurpose --throughput-mode bursting --encrypted. After creation, create mount targets for each AZ and adjust security groups. A common mistake is forgetting mount targets in the AZ of the EC2 instance, which makes the file system unreachable from that instance. Key takeaway: create the file system, set modes, and ensure mount targets and security group rules align with your compute placement. Creating an EFS File System (Console & CLI) means choose performance and throughput modes, enable encryption if needed, and ensure mount targets are created in the azs where compute runs.. In practical terms, essential configuration steps and a simplified cli example.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mounting EFS to an EC2 instance is a practical, repeatable process. First, install the amazon-efs-utils package so you can use the mount helper. Then create a local directory to use as the mount point. Use the EFS file system ID and mount with TLS to encrypt traffic in transit. Choosing the right storage service depends on protocol requirements, access patterns, and operating system needs. Amazon S3 is object storage accessed via HTTP and is ideal for unstructured content, backups, and data lakes where POSIX semantics are not required. Amazon EBS is block storage attached to a single EC2 instance, offering low-latency block device semantics for operating systems and databases. Amazon EFS is a shared NFS file system for Linux workloads needing concurrent POSIX file access and multi-AZ durability. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB and Windows-native features, while FSx for Lustre serves parallel, high-throughput compute clusters. A concrete decision example: a relational database needs EBS for single-instance block access; a web cluster serving uploaded images that require POSIX semantics uses EFS; a Windows file share with AD-integrated permissions uses FSx for Windows; an HPC job processing petabytes in parallel with S3-backed datasets uses FSx for Lustre. A common mistake is picking S3 because of cost without recognizing that the application expects POSIX behavior like atomic renames. Key takeaway: match protocol and semantics first, then performance profile, and finally cost and management trade-offs.

Let's summarize three core concepts to remember. First, a shared file system enables multiple compute instances to concurrently access the same files with standard file semantics. This is essential for applications that rely on POSIX or native file features. Second, Amazon EFS is a managed NFS file system that scales elastically and offers performance and throughput modes; select General Purpose for latency-sensitive tasks and Max input and output or provisioned throughput when aggregate throughput or steady performance is required. Third, the FSx family offers specialized options: FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB and Windows-native features with Active Directory integration, while FSx for Lustre targets high-performance parallel workloads and can integrate with object storage for dataset staging. Keep these concepts in mind when you design storage architecture: match protocol and semantics first, then align performance and security requirements.
